$PRME | FDA proposes adding new gene variants to an approved editing BLA without new clinical trials 🚨

On October 27, 2026, FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research issued a draft guidance, "Individualized Human Genome Editing Products: Considerations for BLA Submission and Postapproval Management".

It covers monogenic diseases where patients carry different pathogenic variants in the same gene. A single BLA under section 351(a) of the PHS Act can hold multiple product variants, each tailored to one mutation, bounded by a concept the guidance introduces: the individualized feature space, or IFS, the declared limits within which the editing components may vary.

Strength, formulation, the in vivo delivery vehicle such as the lipid nanoparticle, and the ex vivo cell type should remain constant across variants. What varies is typically the guide RNA. A variant falling inside the established IFS counts as a manufacturing change rather than a new product, submitted as a BLA supplement with in vitro activity data showing on-target editing at or above a clinically established threshold, plus NGS-based on-target and off-target safety data for each guide and editor combination. Where the link between in vitro data and clinical safety and effectiveness is well understood, FDA generally does not expect clinical data for those additions, and recommends an approved postapproval change management protocol under 21 CFR 601.12(e). Widening the IFS requires a prior approval supplement, and validation designed to cover the full IFS generally avoids revalidating per variant.

Prime Medicine's liver franchise is built on that architecture. The universal liver LNP holds formulation, GalNAc targeting ligand and prime editor mRNA constant and swaps only the guide RNAs, the same split FDA draws between fixed elements and variable features. PM577a targets ATP7B H1069Q, roughly 30 to 50 percent of Wilson disease alleles in the United States and Europe, with the first patient dosed in October 2026 and a follow-on R778L candidate in preclinical development. Those additional ATP7B variants could reach the label as supplements to the same application rather than as separate programs, sharply lowering the marginal cost of each additional mutation.

Three things set the ceiling. The IFS should be supported primarily by clinical data, and the applicant should justify that the variants actually studied span the entire proposed space, with extrapolation judged case by case on natural history, genotype-phenotype associations and genotype-driven safety factors, including variants producing no protein, where immunogenicity risk may rise. One studied variant supports a narrow space, not an open one. The framework also scales within a single gene and a single editing outcome, so the Wilson disease franchise and the SERPINA1 program behind PM647 would not share an IFS. And FDA's worked example varies a single guide RNA spacer, while a pegRNA varies across spacer, primer binding site and RT template, with a nicking guide alongside, so how wide a space that supports is unsettled.

The mechanism line falls where prime editing sits. Without naming it, FDA states that an editor relying on a reverse transcriptase does not belong in the same BLA as a base editor, since off-target and immunogenicity risks differ, and that adding one to an approved base editing product would be a new product requiring a new BLA. RT-based editing is treated as its own mechanistic class, which bounds what can later be folded into one application and equally keeps base editing BLAs from absorbing prime editors.

Whenever I look at a quantum computing roadmap, the first thing to tear apart is the physical qubits vs logical qubits discussion. It takes a lot of noisy physical qubits to build one error-corrected logical qubit, but we are getting better at it, though it’s still a hard comparison given that error distances and many other factors come into play to determine what will actually run on a quantum machine.
In October 2026, Google Quantum AI published a paper in Science (arXiv preprint) demonstrating magic state cultivation on its superconducting Willow processor:
“Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts).”
 
Why do we care?
If you build a fault-tolerant quantum computer with a thousand logical qubits, you do not get to use all thousand of them to run your chemistry simulation or your cryptography algorithm. According to some estimates, as Google Quantum AI research scientist Emma Rosenfeld and quantum software engineer Craig Gidney noted in Google's announcement, "up to 95% of a quantum computer’s entire capacity might need to be dedicated to making" states called magic states, leaving only a small part of the chip to actually run your program.
Every time your algorithm executes a key non-classical operation (a T gate or a Toffoli gate), it consumes one of those magic states and destroys it. So the background “magic state” factory has to run continuously for the entire duration of the computation.
To understand why this paper matters, we need to untangle 😏 two things first:
why a single quantum gate requires a giant factory in the first place,
the difference between error mitigation, post-selection, and error correction.
What a Toffoli gate is, and why it costs so much
When a hardware company reports qubit quality, it reports how accurately it can flip a single qubit (one-qubit gate fidelity) and how accurately two qubits can interact (two-qubit gate fidelity). These are the native operations the hardware performs.
These benchmarks are still important. But now, there are new ways we can think about reporting the error rate of calculations overall.
To really use the power of quantum computers, we need complex operations, and one to know is the Toffoli gate: a three-qubit operation where two control qubits flip a target qubit only when both controls are in state 1. In standard fault-tolerant compilations of the Toffoli gate, it decomposes into six CNOT gates and seven T gates (plus a few single-qubit Clifford gates, or four T gates with measurement-assisted shortcuts).
A CNOT is a Clifford gate. Clifford gates are the cheap(ish) ones. They include the operations you hear about most: putting a qubit into superposition (Hadamard), entangling two qubits (CNOT), and rotating a qubit’s phase by 90 degrees (the S gate). Clifford gates are cheap because common error-correcting codes let you perform them with low overhead: either transversally, meaning you apply the physical gate independently to each of the physical qubits that encode your logical qubit so a single fault doesn’t spread.
A T gate is a non-Clifford gate (a 45-degree phase rotation around the Z axis of the Bloch sphere), and this causes a problem for us.
Why can't we build quantum algorithms out of Clifford gates alone?
The Gottesman-Knill Theorem: Any quantum circuit built purely out of Clifford gates, no matter how entangled it looks, can be simulated efficiently in polynomial time on a normal classical laptop.
The Eastin-Knill Theorem: No quantum error-correcting code can implement a universal set of quantum gates using only easy, fault-tolerant transversal operations.
 
So you see the trap.
To do anything a classical computer cannot do, your circuit must include non-Clifford gates like the T gate or the Toffoli gate. If your error-correcting code makes Clifford gates cheap and transversal, Eastin-Knill guarantees that your non-Clifford T gate cannot be transversal in that same code.
In 2004, Sergey Bravyi and Alexei Kitaev proposed a way out of this mess: magic state distillation. Instead of applying the T gate directly to your fragile encoded data, you prepare a special ancillary quantum state called a magic state, create a large batch of noisy copies, and run an error-filtering Clifford circuit across them to distill one high-purity magic state after several rounds. You then teleport that magic state to execute a single T gate, consuming the magic state in the process.
Because magic state distillation takes multiple logical qubits and multiple code cycles, every Toffoli gate in a fault-tolerant algorithm requires a dedicated "factory" running in the background. Traditional surface-code distillation factories require thousands of physical qubits per factory.
When a large fault-tolerant algorithm like breaking a 256-bit elliptic-curve key (secp256k1, used in Bitcoin) requires roughly 40 million to 1.7 billion Toffoli gates depending on how you trade off qubit count against circuit depth, that factory can easily eat 95% of the machine (though the exact percentage changes with algorithm, code choice, and qubits, this gives you a sense of the order of magnitude we’re talking about).
Error Mitigation vs. Post-Selection vs. Error Correction
Before we look at how Google shrunk that factory, I need to clear up three terms that constantly get blurred together:
Error Mitigation (Classical Post-Processing): You run a noisy quantum circuit with zero redundancy, let physical errors happen, and use extra circuit runs and classical post-processing to estimate the clean result (for example, running the circuit at different noise levels so a classical computer can extrapolate what the noise-free average might have looked like). Mitigation works for short, shallow NISQ experiments.
Error Detection and Post-Selection (Throwing Away Failed Runs): You encode your qubits into a small code that can detect whether an error occurred, without having enough to fix it on the fly. Whenever we flag an error, you abort the shot, throw that run in the trash, and only keep the runs that finish with zero detected faults.
True Fault-Tolerant Error Correction (Real-Time Repair): You encode your logical qubits with enough redundancy that a real-time classical decoder can both spot where errors happened and actively correct them on the fly, cycle after cycle, keeping a single computation alive across millions or billions of sequential gates.
Why does that distinction matter so much? First, the marketing tends to blur these lines, so it’s something to know up front. But also because if you try to rely on post-selection across an entire deep quantum algorithm, you hit an exponential wall. Even if each step has a 99% chance of succeeding, the probability of surviving 10,000 sequential steps without a single error is 0.99¹⁰⁰⁰⁰, which is basically zero. You would throw away runs until the sun burned out.
How Magic State Cultivation Uses Post-Selection
In September 2024, Google Quantum AI researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones published a theory paper titled Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates.
Their insight took a bit of the middle ground: post-selection only fails when a circuit is deep; when a preparation circuit is tiny and only tens of 35-nanosecond gate layers deep, throwing away bad runs is way cheaper than repairing them.
In that paper, they calculated on a simulator that growing a magic state inside a tiny post-selected "nursery" and then handing it over to a standard surface code could fit inside the footprint of a normal logical gate, use an order of magnitude fewer qubit-rounds than traditional distillation, and reach error rates low enough that "further magic state distillation may never be needed in practice."
 
Traditional multi-stage surface-code distillation vs. Google Willow's two-stage Magic State Cultivation and Grafting pipeline
In December 2025, the Google Quantum AI team released a preprint putting that theoretical blueprint on silicon, and in October 2026 the peer-reviewed results were published in Science. By building and running the pipeline on their 105-qubit superconducting Willow processor, they demonstrated three important things:
Growing a magic state with 99.99(1)% fidelity and 40x error reduction: Raw magic states injected onto Willow start with an error rate around 1 in 230 (~99.56% fidelity, or 4.4 × 10⁻³ error). Willow grows and checks each magic state inside a tiny distance-3 color-code “nursery” using about a dozen physical qubits. If any check flags an error during growth or verification, Willow immediately discards that shot and resets. Across the full multi-round cultivation and tomography circuit, the 8% of attempts that survive reach a logical fidelity of 99.99(1)%.
A proof-of-principle “grafting” handoff: A purified magic state sitting inside a tiny color-code nursery cannot run a large algorithm on its own; it has to “escape” into a larger surface-code patch where the main computation happens, a delicate step where we can add a lot more error in the process. Using 54 of Willow's 105 qubits, the team demonstrated a proof-of-principle grafting handoff into a distance-5 hybrid code (decoded offline afterward).
Cubic error scaling means better hardware makes cultivation improve even faster: The team projects from their circuit simulations that if Willow's physical gate noise improves by 2x, the cultivated magic state error upper bound should drop by roughly 5x to 8x.
The Catch: Why Reset Speed and Measurement Matters Now
Two practical hardware lessons stand out from this experiment.
Below we break down the catches behind Google’s Willow numbers and run an apples-to-apples comparison across competing hardware roadmaps, the math behind Quantinuum’s "100x lower error" Helios headline, plus how different types of qubits are trying to simplify error correction hardware first.

Folks (see screenshot) have made the point that the labs only goal is to sell more tokens.

So I'll update what I said in the quote tweet to be more precise: if the labs' goal/long term approach is to sell/provide universal access to fixed-unit cost tokens, they will fail.

If they labs want to succeed, the goal of their DeployCo's and (their strategy writ large) needs to be to

1) develop a predictive model that understands which pockets of the economy, at any time, produce the highest returns to frontier intelligence and what those returns are, and

2) build the deployment meta-learner (a continual learning system) that allows them to realize those returns faster, more reliably, and in more valuable areas than anyone else. 

Building/improving 1) tells the labs where to allocate capital (at the limit, compute) and how much to allocate, Building/improving 2) expands the pockets of economic complexity from which they can practically realize returns from allocating machine intelligence (areas of the economy that appear "API complete" to them)

Crucially, 2) provides the ground truth signals that allows 1) to become more predictive over time.

You could optimistically say that developing these capabilities will allow the labs to power positive sum intelligence auctions (to price tokens dynamically in a way that's win, win, win for everyone involved) across the economy. But for variety of reasons (technical, economic, political) I think this is unlikely to work.

The reality instead, is that continuous vertical integration over the (always evolving) distribution of the economy with the highest returns to intelligence—high and increasing task complexity—is the only way they can capture durable value. And these capabilities are what they need to transition to and power this vertically integrated business model.

The labs have realized that selling/provide universal access to frontier tokens AND trying to durably capture value from those tokens (which is required to attract the capital necessary to stay on the frontier in the first place) means continuously competing with your best customers: those that have high returns to frontier tokens.

They know this isn't a coherent strategy and that they need to change course. Selling your alpha to competitors means eroding your long term returns, so you will rationally stop or be forced, by the capital markets, to stop doing that.

(If the logic here is confusing, see @hypersoren's excellent piece below that provides a much clearer, analytical explanation for why you cannot capture durable value by selling tokens. I'm sure, or at least hope, that everyone important at the labs has read and/or understands this.

https://t.co/8euQ0IBy5n)

Ok, so, now that they've decided that this is no longer tenable, and that they need to create and privately monetize machine intelligence via automated capital allocation and deployment capabilities, what does that mean for the rest of us?

Knowing this, the rational move for everyone else is to not fall for the trap of buying from (and in the process) leaking your scarce/singular context to your future competitors (the labs). This is true at the level of individuals, firms, and economies!

Cursor gave us a nice existence proof for what you don't want to happen to the rest of the economy. This supplier, to competitor, to existential threat dynamic was clearest to Cursor first, which is why you saw them post-train their own model first. Unfortunately, in their case, they realized it was already too late, and that the only economically rational decision was to sell to the lab overlords.

They sold because they knew that, in coding, the only only thing standing in the way of the labs getting access to the the scarce context necessary to produce a superior offering was capital. And capital was something the labs of course had in spades. Abundant capital (compute) allowed them to 1) scale pre-training and post training to the point where their coding products were immediately at parity with whatever Cursor could offer, and 2) subsidize tokens such that all of the new context/signal necessary to stay on the frontier/be more useful than Cursor was produced in their harnesses. "Harness / model co-optimization", etc.

Many smart people have extrapolated/generalized this as the likely end state of everything (not just coding), and come to the conclusion that they are better off joining the labs rather than trying to compete with them.

Luckily, lab access to the scarce context necessary to allocate capital / compete / effectively vertically integrate in other areas with high returns to intelligence seems to be more bottlenecked by humans/trust/time than compute/capital, which means that if everyone starts acting in their own best interest, we will make it out of this alive.

(see Dwarkesh's Data Black Hole, Tom Reed's Goodhart Singularity, @anjali_shriva and @joodalooped's RLWD pieces for intuition here)

The labs (not because they are bad people, but because capitalism/markets are a brutal natural selection machine) have of course been finding every way they can to surmount these diffusion bottlenecks, buy themselves more time, obviate these bottlenecks all together, etc. DeployCos, Thrive Holdings, calls to slow development by fearmongering about RSI, data retention under the guise of safety, regulatory capture, are some examples, but there are many more.

We will see their desperation accelerate as open-source catches up to the frontier and as this logic becomes increasingly legible to everyone. You'll see them using capital and aggressive political narratives to try to brute force/coerce these bottlenecks or obviate them. Again this is not because they are bad people, it's just what they need to do to survive.

In other words, the market will work as it should and reallocate capital from the labs to other economic actors, as long as we let it! We mustn't let lab narratives around RSI, existential risk etc. give them the capital, time or political ammunition they need to make the economy look like a central planner or the country look like one with a natural resource curse.

Luckily, particularly in the past few weeks, it seems savvy economic actors are already well aware of what's going on and are finally publicly calling the labs' bluff (with words and capital). 

All of a sudden, everyone is post-training their own models, talking about the importance of an open eco-system and the existential need to own/control your proprietary learning loops (context, evals, selection infra)

CEOs like @satyanadella and @nikesharora are making it abundantly clear that this is existential (and that, of course, they are the ones who can help you!)

And, luckily, many have known this since the beginning. Firms like @formationbio architected themselves from day one (pre-ChatGPT) around proprietary learning loops that they do not rent from others OR rent to others. They instead are architected to monetize their search and learning in ways that cannot be distilled and commoditized. Structuring themselves this way is what will allow them to attract and deploy the capital necessary to provide durable value to the patients they hope to serve!

Even Lilly owns their own cluster, is hiring for 100s of AI related roles (yes, I've been monitoring their job board), and is partnering with the non-frontier lab AI entities that are incentive aligned to provide capabilities without becoming competition.

So we should be alright, if we don't let the psychosis swallow us.

AMD’s long standing investment in chiplet architectures is delivering structural advantages over @nvidia  in the AI accelerator market, particularly visible in the Instinct MI455X versus Rubin comparison. AMD pioneered disaggregated designs with its EPYC and Ryzen lines, separating high performance compute dies from I/O and cache functions so that each can use the optimal process node. Leading edge nodes are used only where density and performance matter most, and more mature higher yield nodes are used elsewhere. This modular approach, stitched together via Infinity Fabric and advanced packaging, produces higher manufacturing yields on smaller dies, lower cost per yielded transistor, faster product iteration, and the ability to scale capacity simply by adding more chiplets. 

$NVDA  has adopted multi die packaging, as in Blackwell’s two dies and Rubin’s dual compute dies joined by NV HBI, primarily as a workaround for reticle size limits, but it remains less modular and more performance oriented at the expense of cost and flexibility. Analysts note that AMD’s greater experience with chiplets can offset some interconnect power and performance penalties while enabling broader product segmentation and independent optimization of compute, memory, and I/O.

These benefits appear most clearly in memory capacity and rack scale scaling. The MI455X, built from roughly two dozen chiplets including eight compute dies on TSMC 2 nm, fabric and cache dies on 3 nm, and associated I/O, supports 12 stacks of HBM4 for 432 GB of capacity and 23.3 TB/s peak bandwidth. By contrast, NVIDIA’s Rubin uses fewer stacks, typically eight, for 288 GB and lower effective bandwidth after the company reduced HBM4 pin speed from 11.7 Gbps to 9.3 Gbps. At the system level, a 72 GPU AMD Helios rack pools roughly 31 TB of HBM4 versus about 20.7 TB in NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72. The extra capacity and bandwidth density support larger models, longer contexts, and higher concurrency inference with less reliance on multi GPU sharding or offload, exactly the workloads that dominate current AI demand. Chiplet modularity also allows AMD to partition a single package into one large GPU, two smaller ones, or up to eight virtualized accelerators, adding deployment flexibility that a more rigidly paired multi die design does not match as easily.

NVIDIA retains strengths in peak low precision matrix throughput on certain formats, its tightly integrated CUDA software ecosystem, and scale up networking maturity. AMD’s chiplet strategy, however, positions it as the more cost effective and capacity scalable alternative at a time when memory capacity and system level memory pools are becoming primary constraints for frontier models. The manufacturing flexibility of smaller dies also supports faster volume ramps once process yields stabilize, which matters as both companies fight for limited advanced packaging and HBM supply.

On October 6, 2026, during a visit to Taipei and South Korea, AMD CEO Lisa Su told reporters that the company had already increased its supply through 2026 but that demand remained higher than available output. She stated that AMD plans to substantially increase its supply in 2027 and that the company could still use more capacity. Dr. Su explained that AMD now plans three to five years ahead with partners, rather than one or two years, so that wafer, packaging, and substrate capacity can expand in coordinated fashion. She met with Foxconn and planned meetings with TSMC, and she was scheduled to travel to South Korea to engage memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix. Su also indicated that AMD is increasing its multi billion dollar investment in the Taiwan supply chain beyond the more than 10 billion dollar commitment announced earlier in the year, underscoring the company’s effort to convert design advantages into higher volumes of Instinct GPUs and EPYC CPUs to meet sustained AI demand.

While most of the market chased peak training FLOPS and dense GPU clusters, Helion materializes the practical requirement for abundant general purpose cores to keep concurrent agents productive at scale, pairing the chiplet modularity of Venice with the high bandwidth HBM pools on the accelerator side.
